newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Goldman sees U.S. flows into non-US/emerging mkts.
newsitem.headline: Goldman sees U.S. flows into non-US/emerging mkts.

text.p: Investors in the United States are expected to continue pouring money into non-U.S. markets, and particularly emerging markets, Goldman Sachs partner and head of global investment research Steven Einhorn said.
"I think the trend of international investing is absolutely a sustainable one," he told reporters here.

"U.S. investors today have about five percent of their equity holdings outside of the U.S...Every pension fund, public or private, suggests they want 10 or 15 percent of their equity asset base outside of the U.S.," Einhorn said.

He said the move had already started in the first quarter of 1996 when $90 billion, at an annual rate, left the United States to go into non U.S. markets. About 20 percent of that found its way into emerging markets.

"I think it is absolutely a trend that is in place, sustainable and will grow with time with the benefit of, in particular, emerging markets -- Latin America, Asia and eventually Eastern Europe," he said.
But Goldman is underweighted in Asian emerging markets, excluding Hong Kong, due to a slowdown in economic activity.

"The concern that we would have with respect to Asia, not Hong Kong, has to be first economic growth is slowing and there is a question as to whether the slowing is cyclical slowing or something more sustainable," said Einhorn.

In order for Goldman to change its weighting, Einhorn said there would need to be some stability and reacceleration in economic growth. "Secondly there is some element of inflation acceleration and we need to see that subside."
"Thirdly, profit growth has slowed. We need to see that stabilise and go back up," Einhorn added.
But he said Goldman was overweight in Hong Kong, with stocks expected to reap higher returns than U.S. stocks due to more substantial profit growth and flows from the United States.
"If the U.S. market can do 10 percent... it is not unreasonable to think 15 percent returns in Hong Kong in 1997," he said.
